title: 2 Samuel 12:26–31
context: The narrative returns to the siege of Rabbah begun in 11:1. Joab captures the royal city, or the city of waters, and urges David to come and take the city so that it will not be named after Joab. David does so, takes the heavy crown, carries off plunder and puts the people to work. The account rounds off the frame around the Bathsheba story: the war in which Uriah died is concluded. Verse 31 is translated in different ways: many modern versions describe forced labor with saws, picks and axes and at the brick kilns, while some older renderings imply harsher treatment. The parallel in 1 Chronicles 20:3 has its own wording. Both traditions read the passage soberly, noting that David’s outward success does not cancel the judgment announced in 12:10–12.

verses.text: Now Joab fought against Rabbah of the children of Ammon, and took the royal city.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joab fights against Rabbah of the Ammonites and takes the royal city. The narrative returns to the siege begun in 11:1.

Arminian readers note that the frame of the war returns, reminding readers that life and duty continued while David’s sin unfolded, and that David’s absence from the battle began this story.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that this account may well be a return to events that happened during or soon after the period narrated in chapters 11–12, since the narrator often arranges material thematically; the chronology is not stated.

Both traditions read the closing war account as completing the frame around the Bathsheba narrative.

verses.text: Joab sent messengers to David, and said, “I have fought against Rabbah. Yes, I have taken the city of waters.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joab sends messengers to David saying he has fought against Rabbah and taken the city of waters. Joab has secured a key part of the city.

Arminian readers note that Joab has done the work the king should have led, which quietly echoes the opening contrast between the king who stayed home and the army in the field.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the city of waters likely refers to the part of Rabbah controlling its water supply, though the exact meaning is uncertain; its capture would make the fall of the city only a matter of time.

Both traditions read the report as preparing for David’s return to lead the final assault.

verses.text: Now therefore gather the rest of the people together, and encamp against the city and take it; lest I take the city, and it be called by my name.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Joab urges David to gather the remaining troops and take the city, lest Joab take it and it be named after him. Joab defers to the king.

Arminian readers note that Joab protects the king’s honor, perhaps out of loyalty and perhaps from political calculation, and that the king’s honor now depends on others’ actions.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the irony that the king who neglected his duty at the start of chapter 11 must now be summoned to claim credit for a victory largely won by others, a gentle rebuke embedded in the narrative.

Both traditions read Joab’s request as a sign of the shifting relationships in David’s court after the Uriah affair.

verses.text: David gathered all the people together and went to Rabbah, and fought against it and took it.
verses.arminianNotes:
David gathers the people, goes to Rabbah, fights and takes it. David returns to the battlefield.

Arminian readers note that David now does what he should have done at the beginning, and that renewed faithfulness after repentance is possible and good, though it does not undo past wrongs.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God grants David victory even after his grave sin, a sign of God’s continued faithfulness to his covenant with David (7:15), though the judgment announced by Nathan still stands.

Both traditions see David’s return to his duty as fitting, while recognizing that outward success does not erase the consequences God has decreed.

verses.text: He took the crown of their king from off his head; and its weight was a talent of gold, and in it were precious stones; and it was set on David’s head. He brought a great quantity of plunder out of the city.
verses.arminianNotes:
David takes the crown from their king’s head, which weighs a talent of gold with precious stones, and it is placed on David’s head; he also takes much plunder. The crown is very heavy.

Arminian readers note that the weight of the crown, about a talent, has led some interpreters to suggest it was worn only ceremonially, and that David’s outward triumph contrasts with the inward sorrow of chapter 12.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the Hebrew word rendered their king can also be read as Milcom, the Ammonite god (compare 1 Kings 11:5), and some translations take it that way; the crown may then have adorned an idol. The text allows either reading.

Both traditions read the victory soberly, aware of the judgment hanging over David’s house.

verses.text: He brought out the people who were in it, and put them to work under saws, under iron picks, under axes of iron, and made them go to the brick kiln; and he did so to all the cities of the children of Ammon. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
David brings out the people and puts them to work with saws, iron picks and axes, and at the brick kilns, and does so to all the Ammonite cities, then returns with the people to Jerusalem. The account closes the war.

Arminian readers note that the WEB, like many modern versions, describes forced labor, while some older translations imply harsh treatment or torture; the wording is debated and readers should hold their conclusion carefully.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the Hebrew is difficult and that the parallel in 1 Chronicles 20:3 has its own wording; interpreters differ on whether forced labor or harsher punishment is meant, and the text should not be pressed beyond what is clear.

Both traditions read the conclusion soberly and do not hold it up as a model for imitation.
